Module 3 | Program Evaluation and Causal Inference¶

Day 3 | Group Assignment | Questions¶

Hi Team! 👋

As discussed, these questions will help you practice your understanding of causal inference, as well as various econometric designs and methods.

Keep in mind that in real-world applications, when you're faced with business questions, the questions themselves won't dictate which econometric method you should use. It's up to you to determine the most appropriate method for assessing and addressing your specific business questions.

While the revised questions shouldn't be too difficult to solve, given what you've learned, one challenge you'll need to tackle is deciding which econometric method will best help you answer the given questions.

Enjoy!

Big Question 1.

BUSINESS CONTEXT

An organization increased its cap on weekly earnings covered by worker's compensation.¶

As a respected data scientist in the field, you have been hired as a consultant by the company. They want to know if this new strategy has led workers to spend more time unemployed.¶

If benefits are not generous enough, workers may sue companies for on-the-job injuries. However, overly generous benefits could create moral hazard issues, encouraging workers to be more reckless on the job or falsely claim that off-the-job injuries occurred at work.¶

The primary outcome variable you are concerned with is log_duration, which represents the logged duration (in weeks) of worker's compensation benefits. You log it because the variable is fairly skewed—most people are unemployed for a few weeks, with some remaining unemployed for an extended period.¶

The strategy was designed so that the cap increase would not affect low-earning workers but would impact high-earning workers. Therefore, you use low-earning workers as your control group and high-earning workers as your treatment group.¶

Based on your analysis using econometric methods of your choice, what is your assessment? Did the policy cause an increase in the duration of unemployment following a workplace injury? If so, by how much?¶

LIST of VARIABLES


  • duration: Duration of unemployment benefits, measured in weeks

  • log_duration: Logged version of duration

  • after_change: Categorical variable marking if the observation happened before (0) or after (1) the policy change in 1980. This serves as our time (or before/after variable)

  • high_earning: Categorical variable marking if the observation is a low (0) or high (1) earner. This is our group (or treatment/control) variable

  • male: Categorical variable for gender (1 = male)

  • married: Categorical variable for marital status (1 = married)

  • age: Age of the individual

  • hospitalized: Indicator variable for hospitalization (1 = hospitalized)

  • industry: Categorical variable for types of industry (1 = manufacturing, 2 = construction, 3 = other)

  • injury_type: Categorical variable for different types of injuries (1-8)

  • log_pre_wage: Logged version of wage prior to filing a claim

Sensitivity Analysis¶

In [15]:
model_simple =\
(
    smf
    .ols(formula = "log_duration ~ high_earning * after_change",
         data = data1_CLEANED)
    .fit()
)
In [16]:
model_with_covariates =\
(
    smf
    .ols(formula = "log_duration ~ high_earning * after_change + " # main terms of interest for the interaction term
                   "male + married + age + hospitalized + industry + injury_type + log_pre_wage", # covariates
         data = data1_CLEANED)
    .fit()
)
In [17]:
model_with_boundary =\
(
    smf
    .ols(formula = "log_duration ~ high_earning * after_change * married", # three-way interactions
         data = data1_CLEANED)
    .fit()
)
In [18]:
model_with_boudnary_covariates =\
(
    smf
    .ols(formula = "log_duration ~ high_earning * after_change * married + " # main terms of interest for the interaction term
                   "male + age + hospitalized + industry + injury_type + log_pre_wage", # covariates
         data = data1_CLEANED)
    .fit()
)

Visualization or Modeling

Answer: Across robust specifications (Models 1–2), the policy caused high-earning workers to spend on average *around 1.2 weeks (~6 working days) longer* on unemployment benefits compared to low earners — a statistically significant moral hazard effect. Models 3–4 are insignificant once marital status is introduced, but the core finding holds across the two primary specifications.

Big Question 2.

BUSINESS CONTEXT

You are a policymaker in the field of educational policy.¶

At the beginning of a school year, students take an entrance exam. Those who score 70 or below are automatically enrolled in a free tutoring program and receive assistance throughout the year. At the end of the school year, students take a final test, or exit exam (with a maximum of 100 points), to measure their overall learning.¶

Fortunately, as a policymaker, you possess expertise in econometric designs and methods. Using your expertise, please assess whether the tutoring program had a causal impact on students' improvement in test scores. If so, by how much?¶

LIST of VARIABLES

  • id: Student ID

* `tutoring`: Categorical variable showing whether the student was enrolled in the tutoring program
  • entrance_exam: Student's entrance exam score (out of 100)

  • exit_exam: Student's exit exam score (out of 100)

Prepare Kernel Weights¶

In [37]:
def kernel_weights(R, c, h):
    indicator = (np.abs(R - c) <= h).astype(float)
    return indicator * (1 - np.abs(R - c) / h)
In [38]:
(
    plt
    .scatter(data2["entrance_exam"], # x-axis
             kernel_weights(data2["entrance_exam"],
                            c = 0,
                            h = 5), # y-axis
            )
)

Answer: The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) of the tutoring program is approximately 14 percentage points — students who received tutoring scored 14 points higher on their exit exam compared to those who did not.

Big Question 3.

BUSINESS CONTEXT

Consider that you are a data scientist working at the World Bank. You are currently working on analyzing the economic impact of the 1990 German reunification. Specifically, you want to estimate the impact of the reunification on the GDP per capita of West Germany, by comparing the post-reunification trajectory of West Germany to a synthetic control region constructed from other countries.¶

Outcome Variable: gdp

  • [gdp] GDP per Capita (PPP, 2002 USD): Source: OECD National Accounts (retrieved via the OECD Health Database). Data for West Germany was obtained from Statistisches Bundesamt 2005 (Arbeitskreis “Volkswirtschaftliche Gesamtrechnungen der Lander”) and converted using PPP ¨monetary conversion factors (retrieved from the OECD Health Database).

  • [investOO] Investment Rate: Ratio of real domestic investment (private plus public) to real GDP. The data are reported in five-year averages.

  • [schooling] Schooling: Percentage of secondary school attained in the total population aged 25 and older. The data are reported in five-year increments.

  • [industry] Industry: industry share of value added. Source: World Bank WDI Database 2005 and Statistisches Bundesamt 2005.

  • [infrate] Inflation: annual percentage change in consumer prices (base year 1995).

- [`trade`] `Trade Openness`: Export plus imports as percentage of GDP. 
NOTE:

You have missing values in the outcome variable (GDP per capita). Missing values in covariates (Xs of your choice) are allowed.

IMPORT

In [78]:
data3 =\

Big Question 4.

BUSINESS CONTEXT

A big multinational bank decided to invest in training for its new managers. To measure the effectiveness of the training, the company attempted to randomly select managers for the program. The plan was to compare the engagement scores of employees whose managers were enrolled in the program with those whose managers were not. With proper randomization, this simple comparison would provide the average treatment effect of the training.

Unfortunately, things did not go as planned. Some managers didn’t want to attend the training, so they simply didn’t show up. Others managed to receive the training without being assigned to it. As a result, what was intended to be a randomized study ended up resembling an observational one.

Your goal is to estimate the causal effects: the treatment variable is intervention, and your outcome of interest is engagement_score, which is the average standardized engagement score for that manager’s employees. Beyond the treatment and the outcome, the covariates in this data are as follows:

Variables Collected¶

  • department_id: A unique identifier for the department
  • tenure: The number of years the manager has been with the company (as an employee, not necessarily as a manager)
  • n_of_reports: The number of reports the manager has
  • gender: Categorical variable for manager identified gender
  • role: Job category inside the company
  • department_size: The number of employees in that same department
  • department_score: The average engagement score in that same department
  • last_engagement_score: The average engagement score for that manager in the previous iteration of the engagement survey

Please solve the causal analytic question for the bank using two methods of matching in econometrics: namely, propensity score matching and matching with inverse probability weights.

Provide your workflow of analysis that will lead to answers for the questions given below. It is advisable to write your answers within separate code cells with annotations (either using comments in the code cell or using markdown cells).

Matching with Inverse Probability Weights (IPW)¶

In [68]:
data_z["IPW"] =\
(
    (data_z["intervention"] / data_z["propensity_score"])
    +
    (
        (1 - data_z["intervention"]) / (1 - data_z["propensity_score"])
    )
)

In [71]:
def build_multiple_plots(df, 
                         covariates, 
                         treatment = "intervention"):
    figure =\
    (
        ggplot(df,
               aes(x = covariates,
                   fill = as_discrete(treatment)
                 ) 
              )
        + geom_density(alpha = 0.45) 
        + labs(title = f"Distribution of {covariates} by treatment vs. control groups",
               y = "Density",
               fill = "intervention")        
    )
    return figure

                                      covariates = covariate)

What are the causal effects obtained from the two?

PSM Model (1): The ATE of the training intervention is 0.265 — managers who received training saw their employees' engagement scores increase by 0.265 standard deviations compared to those who did not (p < 0.01).

IPW Model (2): The ATE of the training intervention is 0.271 — managers who received training saw their employees' engagement scores increase by 0.271 standard deviations compared to those who did not (p < 0.01).

Both PSM and IPW estimates are highly consistent, reinforcing the robustness of the causal finding — the training program had a statistically significant positive effect on employee engagement of approximately 0.27 standard deviations.
